content: Giardia lamblia, also known as Lamblia intestinalis or Giardia duodenalis, is a flagellated protozoan parasite that causes the disease giardiasis. Higher Order Classification This organism belongs to the domain Eukaryota, within the group Diplomonadida. It is classified under the family Hexamitidae, subfamily Giardiinae, genus Giardia, and species Giardia lamblia. Natural Reservoir Giardia infects both humans and a variety of animals, including cats, dogs, cows, beavers, deer, and sheep. Microbiological Characteristics Giardia lamblia is a flagellated, microaerophilic parasite. The trophozoite form of Giardia lamblia is pear-shaped and exhibits a unique morphology. It has two identical nuclei, a ventral disc that facilitates adhesion to the host's intestinal lining, and multiple flagella for motility. Genome The genome of Giardia lamblia consists of approximately 2 million base pairs, with an average GC content of 46%. The genetic material is organized into five linear chromosomes. Similar to other eukaryotes, each chromosome is flanked by telomere sequences (5’ TAGGG 3’). Life Cycle Giardia lamblia is a member of the diplomonads. Non-infective Cyst The life cycle begins with the excretion of a non-infective cyst in the feces of an infected host. Once in the environment, the cyst becomes infective. A key feature of the cyst is the presence of four nuclei and retracted cytoplasm. Trophozoite Upon ingestion by a host, the trophozoite emerges in an active state, characterized by feeding and motility. During this stage, the trophozoite undergoes asexual reproduction via longitudinal binary fission. Both trophozoites and cysts are excreted in the feces, but only the cysts are capable of surviving outside the host. Trophozoites are distinguished by their large karyosomes and the absence of peripheral chromatin, giving their two nuclei a halo-like appearance. Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) Observations SEM images show the dorsal surface of a Giardia protozoan isolated from a rat’s intestine. SEM also depicts the mucosal surface of the small intestine of a gerbil infected with Giardia species. SEM captures a Giardia lamblia protozoan in a late stage of cell division, forming a heart-shaped structure as it prepares to divide into two separate organisms. SEM reveals the ventral surface of a Giardia muris trophozoite. SEM highlights the ultrastructural details of an oblong-shaped Giardia cyst. SEM shows a Giardia muris trophozoite adhering to the mucosal surface of a rat’s intestine. SEM captures a Giardia lamblia protozoan in the process of cell division, about to separate into two organisms. SEM depicts a Giardia muris protozoan adhering to the microvillus border of an intestinal epithelial cell. Immunofluorescence Imaging Photomicrographs using indirect immunofluorescence tests demonstrate Giardia lamblia parasites, aiding in the diagnosis of giardiasis. Differential Diagnosis Infections caused by Giardia lamblia must be differentiated from other causes of viral, bacterial, and parasitic gastroenteritis. Small bowel diarrhea: Characterized by watery, voluminous stools with fewer than 5 white blood cells (WBCs) per high-power field. Large bowel diarrhea: Typically mucousy and/or bloody, with less volume but more than 10 WBCs per high-power field. The severity of symptoms can vary, potentially reaching up to 1,000 WBCs per high-power field, depending on the patient’s immune status.
